profile.summary: This is the cell type annotation evaluation published with scTab. A classifier is trained on a corpus built from the CELLxGENE census release 2023-05-15, 22.2 million human cells from 5,052 donors, 56 tissues and 164 cell type labels, and is scored on cells from donors it has never seen. The score is the macro-averaged F1, with a correction from the Cell Ontology so that predicting a finer label than the author annotated is not punished, while predicting a coarser one is. The paper reports this for linear, tree-based and deep models and for three single-cell transformer models, several of them refitted by the authors, and it publishes the processed data with fixed splits and tuned reference models so that others can reuse the same comparison.

As a benchmarking metric, we chose the macro-averaged F1-score (macro F1-score) (Methods) to account for class imbalances and to give each cell type an equal weight in the overall score.
We defined test holdouts based on donor annotation, which we see as a sensible compromise between an entirely random split and a split based on holdout studies.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a classifier can name the cell type of a single cell across the whole human body, not within one tissue, and whether it still does so for donors it has not seen. The authors frame the difficulty as a labelling problem: public corpora annotate at different levels of detail, so an evaluation that treats 164 ontology labels as mutually exclusive rewards a model for copying each study's annotation granularity rather than for telling cell types apart. Their fix is to judge a prediction against the Cell Ontology, which turns the task into predicting a label at least as specific as the author's. A second question the evaluation covers is whether a model knows when it is wrong: uncertainty scores from a deep ensemble are tested for separating correct predictions from incorrect ones, and from cells whose type was never in training.

quotes.text: penalizing a model that predicts CD4-positive, alpha-beta T cell for a cell that is labeled as a T cell results in an evaluation that is biased towards the model being able to mimic the annotation granularity of the data instead of its ability to distinguish cell types

To account for differences in annotation granularity across datasets, we adjusted predictions based on the Cell Ontology to not incur penalties if a model predicts a more fine-grained label than the original author annotation (Methods).
the separation between Group 1 and Group 3 (correct vs absent) gives an estimate of how well the uncertainty scores can be used to detect new/unseen cell types

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The corpus starts from the CELLxGENE census release 2023-05-15, restricted to human data on the 19,331 human protein-coding genes. Five filters follow: only primary data, so that the same cell in an atlas metastudy cannot appear on both sides of the split; only 10x-based assays; the label must be a subtype of the native cell term; each cell type needs at least 5,000 cells and at least 30 donors; and each cell type needs at least seven parent nodes in the ontology, a heuristic to drop very broad labels, which the authors note does not remove all coarse labels. Counts are normalised to 10,000 per cell and log transformed. The result is 22,189,056 cells, 164 cell types, 5,052 donors and 56 tissues, split by donor 70, 15 and 15 per cent into 15,240,192 training, 3,500,032 validation and 3,448,832 test cells. Subsampled training sets are also defined for the scaling experiments, both random and donor-based, from 15 to 100 per cent. The processed corpus is published as a 164 GB download in Merlin dataloader format, with a 0.5 GB minimal subset and the trained checkpoints.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model outputs one label per cell from the 164, and the score is the macro average of the per-class F1 on the held-out donors, so every cell type counts equally regardless of how many cells it has. The ontology correction decides right from wrong: the same label as the author is right, a subtype of the author's label is also right, a parent of the author's label is wrong, and anything else is wrong, with child relations looked up in the Cell Ontology. The paper reports each model as a mean and standard deviation over several fits with different random initialisations, and the supplementary information gives a second version of the same table with bootstrapping across test donors added, which widens the intervals by about an order of magnitude, for example scTab 0.8295 plus or minus 0.0007 over seeds against 0.8300 plus or minus 0.0069 with donor bootstrapping. A separate evaluation aggregates the fine-grained predictions to 31 coarse labels without retraining. Uncertainty is scored by averaging the predicted probabilities of 5 independently trained models, taking one minus the maximum probability as the uncertainty, then measuring the ROC-AUC for separating correct predictions from incorrect ones and from cells of types absent from training, where 1.0 is perfect separation and 0.5 is none. Training and inference cost are reported too, on named hardware.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Download the processed corpus, or the 0.5 GB minimal subset for a first try, and the checkpoints. Install the cellnet package from the repository, either inside the Merlin PyTorch container the authors used or with pip plus the GPU requirements file. The repository holds the data loading code, training scripts, and notebooks for training, for creating the data store and for all the evaluation in the paper, with tutorial notebooks for loading data and for running a trained model. A modern GPU is needed; the authors state that on a desktop without GPU acceleration the runtime will probably exceed several days.

structured.primary_metric: ROC-AUC for separating uncertainty scores from the reference group

quotes.text: Cell types that are present in the training data but which the model predicted wrongly to assess how well wrong predictions can be distinguished from right predictions based on the uncertainty scores.
Cell types that are not present in the training data to assess how well unknown cell types can be identified based on the uncertainty scores provided by scTab.
A ROC-AUC score of 1.0 means that the groups can be perfectly separated and a score of 0.5 means that there is no separation between the groups based on the uncertainty scores
In our case, we averaged the predictions across 5 models.
